patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v3] mm: bypass swap readahead for zswap

version_history.subject: [PATCH v3] mm: bypass swap readahead for zswap

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch bypasses swap readahead for zswap, an in-memory synchronous backend similar to zram. The current implementation of swap readahead can lead to pointless prefetching of pages, causing increased anon residency and page cache thrashing. By bypassing readahead for zswap, the patch aims to reduce this overhead and improve performance. Measurements show significant gains in build time, zswap-in/out rates, and reduced swap readahead hits. The patch reuses existing code and adds a new helper function to check if a swap entry is synchronous.

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Barry Song questioned whether the performance gain from bypassing swap readahead for zswap is dependent on the page-cluster setting, suggesting testing with values 0 and 1 to confirm

Reviewer Barry Song expressed interest in knowing if similar performance gains would be observed when using specific configurations, and suggested adding a mention of the 'page-cluster' configuration to the changelog.

Gave Reviewed-by
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Alexandre,

I assume your configuration is as below?

/ # cat /proc/sys/vm/page-cluster
3
/ # cat /sys/kernel/mm/swap/vma_ra_enabled
true

I am curious whether setting `/proc/sys/vm/page-cluster` to either 0
or 1 would result in the same performance gain on a zswap-enabled

---

The change makes sense to me. I am just curious whether setting those
configurations would result in the same performance gain.

Maybe you can mention the `page-cluster` configuration in the changelog
as well.

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary: The reviewer notes a potential benefit of readahead for compressed swap, citing Kairui's LPC presentation, but acknowledges that this is not currently the case and assumes any future improvements would also apply to zswap.
review_comments.raw_body:
No objection here, I am just thinking about Kairui's LPC presentation
about how compressed swap can (in theory at least) still benefit from
readahead: https://lpc.events/event/20/contributions/2421/attachments/2116/4689/Better%20Anon%20(Swap)%20Readahead%20(2).pdf.

Seems like a big portion of the fault cost is still outside of
decompression and can benefit from readahead, but that isn't the case
today. I assume any future improvements to readahead and re-enabling
for zram would also cover zswap?

review_comments.author: Alexandre Ghiti
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the patch bypasses swap readahead for zswap, but questioned whether it's necessary to do so in all cases, as some systems may not have zswap enabled or may be disk-only.

The reviewer ran additional tests with a workload of kbuild -j16 in a 768M memcg, zswap only, and observed consistent performance gains from bypassing swap readahead for zswap, including reduced build time, zswap-in and zswap-out, and swap readahead pages. The reviewer also confirmed that the results were the same with page-cluster set to 0.

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Barry Song noted that if a high-hit-rate readahead algorithm is developed, it may be necessary to map all readahead folios at the same time in do_swap_page() to avoid increasing total work for synchronous I/O.
review_comments.raw_body:
In that case, if we can develop an accurate readahead algorithm with a
high hit rate for readahead folios, we will probably also need to map
them at the same time, as proposed in [1]. For example, if we readahead
4 folios, we should map them all together in `do_swap_page()`.
Otherwise, the cost of future minor faults can still be comparable to
the decompression cost. Readahead alone would therefore increase the
total work, which can be quite significant for synchronous I/O.

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/CAGsJ_4xM=WnFO-OuwVude-DQ_UkaCi_zF_bXBP9Li5+ZPNy0VQ@mail.gmail.com/

Best Regards
Barry

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Barry Song noted that setting page-cluster = 0 could resolve the issue without the patch, but is still pleased to see the auto-tuning patch.
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks! This seems to be a strong indication that setting
`page-cluster = 0` can also resolve your problem, even without your
patch. :-)

But I'm still glad to see your auto-tuning patch!

Best Regards
Barry

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Nhat Pham noted that bypassing swap readahead for zswap may not be suitable when multiple tenants with different swap backends (compressed synchronous and async IO) coexist on the same host, potentially causing issues.

Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concerns about doing synchronous readahead work in page fault, suggesting it feels wrong and may concentrate work of multiple pagefaults into a single pagefault. They proposed offloading readahead to an asynchronous worker as a potential solution.
review_comments.raw_body:
If every tenants use zswap, yes. But we have tenants with different
kinds of swap backend in the same host (some using compressed
synchronous swap backend, some async IO swap backend).

---

I think we need some smarter readahead work, for sure. I'm just not
quite sure what it'd look like in the end, though.

Doing synchronous readahead work in page fault feels wrong. I chatted
very briefly with Kairui about this. Kairui is trying to come up with
smarter readahead heuristics, but I don't know - even if it's 100%
hitrate, we're concentrating work of multiple pagefaults into a single
pagefault. That sounds off to me?

Crazy idea time - what if instead of skipping readahead for
zswap/zram, we offload it to asynchronous worker (only synchronously
loading the target page)? That'll cancel out the latency issue at
least...?

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Barry Song noted that asynchronous wake-up latency is highly unpredictable and can be much longer than the time it takes to complete mapping and decompression work in do_swap_page(), which makes async zram readahead unreliable without hardware queues.
review_comments.raw_body:
I am quite sure I tried this 3 or 4 months ago, and the
performance was very poor. The problem is that async wake-up
latency is highly unpredictable. For example, do_swap_page()
can complete all the mapping and decompression work in less
than 10 us. However, if we queue the work to an async thread,
its wake-up latency alone could be much longer than 10 us.

Based on my results, async zram readahead only works if we have
hardware queues rather than relying on async threads.

Best Regards
Barry

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Barry Song noted that the patch bypassing swap readahead for zswap might miss some folios in the readahead window that are actually in zswap, and vice versa, but suggested not handling this complexity at this point.
review_comments.raw_body:
Yep, I have no objection to this patch. As I replied to
Alexandre, I was just curious about what would happen if we
set `page-cluster` to 0.

I think Alexandre's autotuning patch looks good overall. We
just have a lot of corner cases to consider. For example, we
might miss zswap and trigger readahead, even though some
folios in the readahead window are actually in zswap. The
opposite could also happen.

However, I don't think we need to handle all this complexity
at this point.

Best Regards
Barry

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary: Gave Acked-by

review_comments.author: Kairui Song
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Kairui Song suggested bypassing swap readahead for zswap, but noted that a better readahead policy is needed to avoid increased unmapping costs. They proposed evaluating shadow as a stronger hint for readahead and implementing proactive aging or a similar approach.
review_comments.raw_body:
That's a really nice POC! We should do that IMO, maybe with better
support for (m)THP readahead too.

We first need a better readahead policy though, or else unmapping
these folios might cost even more.

For the readahead part I'm thinking about evaluating using shadow as a
stronger hint for readahead after MGLRU-FG which helps distribute the
folios based on frequencey more evenly among gens, also with a more
proactive aging (async aging, or maybe lru_gen_imbalanced as Barry
once suggested somewhere) so folios in the same gen with same freq
will be much more likely to be reused. Or something similiar to file
readahead's PG_readahead based readahead. Well more
experiments are needed first though.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 0/6] daxctl: use dax kmem atomic whole-device hotplug

version_history.subject: [PATCH 0/6] daxctl: use dax kmem atomic whole-device hotplug

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/6] libdaxctl: add dax kmem atomic hotplug state accessors
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for atomic whole-device hotplug to the libdaxctl library by introducing an enum and getter/setter functions for accessing the /sys/bus/dax/devices/daxX.Y/state attribute. The new functionality allows users to determine the state of a dax device, such as whether it is online or offline, and set its state accordingly. This patch is part of a larger series that aims to enhance the libdaxctl library with features related to hotplug and memory management.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/6] daxctl: online whole-device memory atomically when available
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the daxctl tool to online whole-device memory atomically when available, rather than onlining each block separately. This approach avoids racing issues with other agents that may be online blocks as they appear. The kernel's daxX.Y/state is used to determine if a device is offline and can be unplugged, allowing for atomic onlineing of the entire device. If another agent has already onlineed memory from the device, the patch will fall back to the per-block path. Additionally, the patch now fails when attempting to online a device with no memory blocks, rather than reporting zero sections already online.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/6] daxctl: offline whole-device memory via atomic unplug when available
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds the ability to offline whole-device memory via atomic unplug when available, ensuring that no agent can online blocks before a later unbind. The kernel offlines and removes the device atomically, leaving it unchanged on failure. If all memory sections are already offline, the operation is a best effort. The patch also updates the 'daxctl list' command to omit 'movable' for devices with no blocks.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/6] daxctl: report whole-device hotplug state in 'daxctl list'
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the 'daxctl list' command to report the whole-device hotplug state as a new field called 'hotplug_state'. The kernel's daxX.Y/state attribute only updates when written, so it can become stale if blocks are toggled individually. To address this issue, the patch introduces a function called 'hotplug_state' that returns a string indicating whether the device is in an inconsistent state or not. If the device is consistent, the function returns a string describing its hotplug state based on its current online and movable memory status.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 5/6] Documentation: describe atomic whole-device hotplug in daxctl man pages
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the documentation of daxctl commands to describe atomic whole-device hotplug functionality. Specifically, it explains how online-memory and offline-memory use the daxX.Y/state attribute where available, and how offlining a device removes its memory blocks in one operation. The 'hotplug_state' attribute is also documented. This patch aims to improve user understanding of daxctl commands and their behavior with atomic whole-device hotplug support.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 6/6] test/daxctl-devices.sh: cycle offline/online to cover unplug and replug
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the test script for daxctl devices to include a cycle of online and offline operations, simulating device unplug and re-plug scenarios. The changes cover cases where a device is brought online from an unplugged state and vice versa, as well as checking that memory can be unplugged even if it's already offline. Additionally, the script checks block counts and kernel memory states after each operation to ensure correctness.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces atomic whole-device hotplug support in daxctl using the dax_kmem attribute, which allows for atomic unplug and plug-and-online of a device. This feature prevents races between daxctl and other agents like udev or auto-online. The patch also adds new 'hotplug_state' reporting to 'daxctl list', which indicates whether the device is in an inconsistent state due to block-level toggling. The patch series includes changes to libdaxctl, daxctl, documentation, and test scripts.

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/page_alloc: validate zonelist slots against concurrent rebuilds

patches_submitted.patch_summary: The patch addresses a concurrency issue in the page allocation mechanism, where an allocation can succeed from a zone it never asked for due to concurrent rebuilds of zonelists. It introduces a new function `zonelist_zone_valid` that rechecks each zone against the highest zone index and nodemask before using it. This ensures that allocations are served from zones they requested, preventing unmovable pages in movable zones.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] mm/page_alloc: detect zonelist rebuilds from memory hot-add
series_items.patch_summary: The patch addresses a spurious allocation failure caused by concurrent GFP_KERNEL and __GFP_THISNODE allocations when onlining the first block of a zone, particularly in configurations that rebuild zonelists after boot. It introduces a gate to check_retry_zonelist() based on CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG, which covers every configuration that rebuilds zonelists after boot.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/2] cgroup/cpuset: use mems_allowed_seq when checking a policy nodemask
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a spurious numa placement miss under certain cpuset/mempolicy combinations by retrying the intersection of mems_allowed and policy nodemask until mems_allowed_seq is stable. The fix involves updating the check in cpuset_nodemask_valid_mems_allowed() to use read_mems_allowed_begin() and read_mems_allowed_retry(). This change ensures that the task's mempolicy and mems_allowed are consistent when checking for valid nodes.

review_comments.author: Vlastimil Babka (SUSE)
review_comments.summary: Identified a potential issue with the comment and code in check_retry_cpuset() and suggested updating them. The patch author disagreed, explaining that they are checking different things.

review_comments.author: Vlastimil Babka (SUSE)
review_comments.summary: Provided a Reviewed-by tag after the patch author addressed some concerns.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses two races in the Linux kernel's memory allocator that can occur when updating zonelists and cpusets concurrently. The first issue arises from a retry mechanism for zonelist updates, which can lead to inconsistent views of state between CPUs. The second problem involves a comparison between a mempolicy nodemask and the current mems_allowed without considering the sequence number, resulting in spurious empty intersections and unnecessary policy relaxations. The patches fix these issues by introducing additional checks and using the correct sequence numbers for updates. These changes aim to prevent allocation failures and ensure that memory policies are correctly enforced.

review_comments.author: Vlastimil (SUSE)
review_comments.summary: Gave Reviewed-by

review_comments.author: Gregory Price (author)
review_comments.summary: Author responded to feedback that the patch's cpuset_nodemask_valid_mems_allowed() function may erroneously drop a nodemask on a race condition, explaining that the loop in this function ensures nodemask and mems_allowed are stable when compared, and that the cookie-check in check_retry_cpuset() runs after the nodemask would already have been dropped.
review_comments.raw_body:
No I don't think so. We're checking different things.

The loop here makes sure nodemask and mems_allowed are stable when
compared so we don't erroneously drop the nodemask on a race.

The cookie-check in check_retry_cpuset() determines whether the entire
allocation should restart.  It runs after the nodemask would already
have been dropped, so it can't catch this race.

~Gregory

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the selftests/mm/madvise.c file where sched_getcpu() can return a CPU number above the maximum allowed, causing sched_setaffinity() to fail. patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 0/8] selftests/mm: add MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT contract tests

version_history.subject: [PATCH 0/8] selftests/mm: add MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT contract tests

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/8] selftests/mm: add MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT contract tests
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds contract tests for the MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT hints in the Linux kernel's selftests/mm module. The tests cover basic behavior, including that MADV_COLD does not populate PTE holes or fault swapped pages back in, and neither hint can be applied to a locked VMA. The tests also verify the swapped-page test works correctly when swap is available. The patch introduces new files for the kselftest harness and a C file containing the test code.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/8] selftests/mm: check that MADV_PAGEOUT skips holes and swapped pages
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two new test cases to the madvise selftest suite in Linux. The tests, 'pageout_skips_pte_hole' and 'pageout_skips_swapped_pte', verify that the MADV_PAGEOUT operation skips over holes in page tables and swapped-out pages, similar to how MADV_COLD operates. This ensures that MADV_PAGEOUT adheres to its contract and does not attempt to populate or fault-in such regions.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/8] selftests/mm: check MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT range handling
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds four new tests to the selftests/mm/madvise test suite to verify the behavior of madvise(2) when dealing with zero-length ranges, unaligned start addresses, and unmapped gaps in the range. The tests check that a zero-length range is accepted, an unaligned start address is rejected, and an unmapped gap in the range causes either MADV_COLD or MADV_PAGEOUT to fail with ENOMEM. Additionally, the patch includes code to pin the test task to a specific CPU to ensure consistent behavior.

review_comments.author: Gregory (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern that the patch's pin_to_current_cpu function fails on large systems due to sched_getcpu() returning a CPU number above CPU_SETSIZE, causing sched_setaffinity() to fail. The author proposes using CPU_ALLOC() to dynamically size the mask instead of relying on a fixed-size mask.

review_comments.author: Sarthak Sharma

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/8] selftests/mm: check that MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT reject hugetlb
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a test to the selftests/mm suite to ensure that madvise(2) fails with EINVAL when attempting to apply MADV_COLD or MADV_PAGEOUT hints to hugetlb memory. The test creates a hugetlb mapping, sets one of its bytes, and then attempts to advise it with both hints, verifying that the calls fail as expected.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 5/8] selftests/mm: check that MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT preserve shared memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a self-test to verify that the MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT hints preserve shared memory, including dirty shared file pages, shared anonymous pages, and SHM_LOCK'd segments. The test checks that these hints do not cause the pages to be evicted or written back, but instead leave them resident. The test requires root privileges to confirm through /proc/kpageflags that a SHM_LOCK'd page is unevictable. The patch adds new functions to map shared memory and page out ranges until they are no longer mapped, and modifies existing functions to pin tasks to specific CPUs and drain LRU batches.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 6/8] selftests/mm: check MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT on partly advised THPs
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds self-tests to verify the behavior of MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT on transparent huge pages (THPs). It checks that a whole PMD-mapped THP is swapped intact, that pages outside the range stay resident after paging out a base page or half of a PMD- or PTE-mapped THP, and that MADV_COLD on half of either THP preserves its contents. The tests also verify that a partly advised THP is split before reclaim, or skipped, to prevent corruption. The patch includes new functions for reserving and mapping aligned memory ranges.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 7/8] selftests/mm: check MADV_PAGEOUT file permissions
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a test to the selftests/mm suite to verify that the MADV_PAGEOUT functionality works correctly with file permissions. The test checks that an owner of a read-only file can evict a clean page, and that unauthorized callers cannot page out shared file pages or private mapping COW pages. The test also verifies that capabilities cannot be used as a substitute for ownership. The patch includes changes to the madvise.c file in the selftests/mm directory.

series_items.subject: [PATCH nfs-utils 1/7] mountd: accept -L for --no-netlink
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the mountd utility where the -L option, which is used to disable netlink, was not properly handled due to its absence from the shortopts string. The fix involves adding the missing 'L' character to the shortopts string, ensuring that the -L option is recognized and functions as intended.

series_items.subject: [PATCH nfs-utils 2/7] mountd: prime the kernel caches over netlink on MOUNT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the mountd service to prime the kernel caches over netlink when a MOUNT request is made, rather than writing directly to /proc channels. This ensures that export state carried only by netlink is not lost. The patch also updates the nl_add_ip_map function to include an expiry TTL and allows cross-mount submounts to be sent over netlink as well.

series_items.subject: [PATCH nfs-utils 3/7] exports: describe the kernel's export features with struct nfsd_export_policy
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the `struct export_features` to `struct nfsd_export_policy` and updates various parts of the code to use the new name consistently. The change is purely cosmetic, as the functionality remains the same. The patch also updates the function `get_export_features()` to return a pointer to `struct nfsd_export_policy` instead of `struct export_features`. This change is part of a larger series of patches that aim to improve the kernel's export features and policy handling.

series_items.subject: [PATCH nfs-utils 4/7] exportfs/mountd/exportd: get export features from the netlink policy
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the NFS utilities to retrieve export features from the netlink policy instead of reading them from /proc/fs/nfsd/export_features. It adds a new function nfsd_export_policy_query() that uses the netlink interface to dump the SET_REQS policy and fills a struct with the maximum attribute value. The patch also introduces set_export_features() and nfsd_nl_load_export_features() functions to seed export features from the policy, and modifies get_export_features() to use the new functions if possible. If the netlink interface is unavailable, get_export_features() still reads /proc/fs/nfsd/export_features as before.

series_items.subject: [PATCH nfs-utils 5/7] nfsref: flush the export caches with cache_flush()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the nfsref code to use libexport's cache_flush() function instead of writing directly to /proc files. The cache_flush() function uses netlink to flush the export caches when available, and falls back to the /proc files otherwise. This change simplifies the code and improves its reliability by providing a more robust way to flush the cache.

series_items.subject: [PATCH nfs-utils 6/7] mountd/exportd: always give pseudo-root directories a path-based uuid
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series modifies the mountd/exportd code in nfs-utils to always use a path-based UUID for pseudo-root directories, rather than relying on the filesystem's own UUID. This change is motivated by issues with exportfs and netlink, where the fs uuid is only used briefly during an exportfs run on a live server.

review_comments.author: Benjamin Coddington
review_comments.summary: Identified a significant issue in the original code and suggested that this change deserves its own Fixes: patch, implying strong support for the patch's intent.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 16 Oct 2026, at 10:15, Jeff Layton wrote:

> c5528f40f9db ("Fix NFSv4 export of tmpfs filesystems") made
> v4root_create() generate a uuid from the path only when export_test()
> says the directory cannot be exported without one, leaving others on
> the filesystem's own uuid. In practice export_test() fails nearly every
> time, so the path-based uuid is what pseudo-root directories get:
>
> - export_test() needs the "-test-client-" auth_domain, which only lives
>   as long as an ip_map entry that references it.
> - With netlink, nothing creates that entry: exportfs's can_test()
>   returns before writing it. The kernel answers ENOENT.
> - With /proc, can_test() creates it, but exportfs's own cache_flush()
>   frees it before mountd rebuilds the pseudo-root.
>
> The fs uuid is only used when mountd rebuilds the pseudo-root during
> the brief window in an exportfs run on a live server, and then that
> directory's filehandle differs from every other time.
>
> Always use the path-based uuid below "/". That keeps what servers have
> done since c5528f40f9db, closes that window, and drops a write to
> /proc/net/rpc/nfsd.export/channel that ran even with netlink.
>
> Also keep uuid_s in scope until export_create() has used it; eep.e_uuid
> pointed at it after the block that declared it had ended.

Oh yeah, nice catch.  This change almost deserves its own Fixes: patch.

Ben

series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a kernel-style MAINTAINERS file and a get_maintainer.pl script to the nfs-utils package. The MAINTAINERS file provides information on how to submit changes, including the mailing list and required Signed-off-by trailer. The get_maintainer.pl script implements match types F/X/N/K and is used by scripts like b4 prep --auto-to-cc to collect To/Cc addresses for patches. The patch also includes new tests and updates Makefile.am and other files.

b4 prep --auto-to-cc
Collecting To/Cc addresses
    + To: Steve Dickson <steved@redhat.com>
    + Cc: open list:NFS-UTILS <linux-nfs@vger.kernel.org>

---

This finds the top of whatever git tree the cwd is in, not the tree
the script lives in.  Running it from a kernel tree:

  $ cd linux
  $ ~/nfs-utils/scripts/get_maintainer.pl -f fs/nfsd/export.c

reads the kernel's MAINTAINERS and prints the knfsd maintainers.

The fallback also leaves "scripts/.." in $topdir, so the -f prefix
strip never matches an absolute path when run from a tarball.

Maybe just always use the script's location:

        return abs_path(dirname(abs_path($0)) . '/..');

b4 runs it from the tree top, so that wouldn't change anything there.

Ben

version_history.subject: [PATCH v1] fuse: don't launder folios of a bad inode

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the FUSE file system where dirty pages are not properly handled when an inode is marked bad. The problem occurs when a writeable file is closed and its inode is marked bad, causing subsequent invalidation to trigger a warning. The fix adds a check in fuse_launder_folio() to return -EIO if the inode is bad.

review_comments.author: Horst Birthelmer
review_comments.summary: Tested and found no issues with this patch. It looks good to go.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Tue, Oct 06, 2026 at 03:51:36AM -0700, Joanne Koong wrote:
> fuse_flush() and fuse_writepages() reject writing back dirty data for
> any inode that has been marked bad, but fuse_launder_folio() doesn't.
> 
> This can cause the following warning in fuse_write_file_get() to
> trigger, as reported by syzbot:
> 
> WARNING: fs/fuse/file.c:2043 at fuse_write_file_get fs/fuse/file.c:2043 [inline]
> WARNING: fs/fuse/file.c:2043 at fuse_iomap_writeback_range+0x7c8/0x18f0 fs/fuse/file.c:2227
> Call Trace:
>     iomap_writeback_folio+0x1526/0x2490 fs/iomap/buffered-io.c:2022
>     fuse_launder_folio+0x17b/0x240 fs/fuse/file.c:2331
>     folio_unmap_invalidate+0x4cd/0x830 mm/truncate.c:634
>     invalidate_inode_pages2_range+0x629/0xb30 mm/truncate.c:726
>     fuse_open+0x5a6/0x770 fs/fuse/file.c:297
> 
> This can be hit on a writeback cache mount:
> 1) a writeable file is open and a buffered write dirties some pages
> 2) another thread opens the same file read-only. fuse_open() passes the
>    bad inode check and sends OPEN to the server.
> 3) a SETATTR reply with the wrong file type marks the inode bad
> 4) the writeable file is closed. Flush and release skip writeback
>    because the inode is bad. The pages stay dirty but the file gets
>    removed from write_files.
> 5) server replies to the OPEN. The reply has no FOPEN_KEEP_CACHE, so
>    fuse_open() calls invalidate_inode_pages2().
> 6) the invalidation finds the dirty pages and calls
>    fuse_launder_folio(), which finds no wriable file and hits the
>    WARN_ON in fuse_write_file_get().
> 
> Instead of trying to write back dirty data for the bad inode,
> fuse_launder_folio() should return -EIO.
> 
> Fixes: 5d069dbe8aaf ("fuse: fix bad inode")
> Reported-by: syzbot+e8200299b0556976e13c@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
> Closes: https://syzkaller.appspot.com/bug?extid=e8200299b0556976e13c
> Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
> Signed-off-by: Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com>
> ---
>  fs/fuse/file.c | 3 +++
>  1 file changed, 3 insertions(+)
> 
> diff --git a/fs/fuse/file.c b/fs/fuse/file.c
> index 6d707f2b3bff..0ef46f6e0267 100644
> --- a/fs/fuse/file.c
> +++ b/fs/fuse/file.c
> @@ -2351,6 +2351,9 @@ static int fuse_launder_folio(struct folio *folio)
>  		.wb_ctx	= &data,
>  	};
>  
> +	if (fuse_is_bad(wpc.inode))
> +		return -EIO;
> +
>  	if (folio_clear_dirty_for_io(folio)) {
>  		err = iomap_writeback_folio(&wpc, folio);
>  		err = fuse_iomap_writeback_submit(&wpc, err);
> -- 
> 2.52.0
> 
> 

Hi Joanne,

I have tested a lot of notification invalidation lately.
Did not hit this one yet.

LGTM!

Feel free to add
Reviewed-by: Horst Birthelmer <hbirthelmer@ddn.com>

Re: memcg stats flushing (WAS "Re: [PATCH] fuse: disable default bdi strictlimiting")
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch aims to improve the performance of memory cgroup (memcg) statistics flushing by reducing cacheline contention and prefetching issues. The author experimented with split rstat trees, but found that it introduced inconsistent and noisy numbers due to cacheline contention. Instead, they propose keeping the existing tree for userspace flushers and adding a 'slim' tree for in-kernel flushers, which would reduce overhead when updating hot stats. Additionally, prefetching the entire stats array on each CPU was found to make flushes 1-7% slower.

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Yosry Ahmed expressed concerns about the implementation of separating in-kernel stats, citing maintenance and complexity issues due to having duplicate stats in two trees. He suggested measuring improvement after eliminating root flushes.

Reviewer Yosry Ahmed expressed surprise at the discovery of spatial prefetching on modern CPUs, which is causing cacheline contention and extra overhead in stat updates.

Reviewer noted that walking the lru list locklessly requires moving it to a local list first, and questioned the necessity of checking if the cgroup is present in the list.
review_comments.raw_body:
I think separating the in-kernel stats is sound in principle, but
implementation and maintenance wise it's not great (especially having
the same stats in two trees). That being said, I didn't see the code
yet, so perhaps I am wrong :)

This is why I think we should measure the improvement after
eliminating root flushes if possible.

---

This is an amazing finding! I am surprised that the CPU would prefetch
a contended cacheline to be honest.

---

IIUC, llist can only be walked locklessly if you first move it to a
local list. But yeah the question was rhetorical, I don't think we
should walk the list to check if the cgroup is there or not.
